html:
The bhakti movement was a wave of devotional religion that began in the Tamil country about 600 CE and spread across all India over the next thousand years. Bhakti means loving devotion to a personal god. Its message was that love counts for more than ritual, learning or birth.

It began with poet-saints who walked from temple to temple and sang in Tamil, not Sanskrit: the twelve Alvars, devoted to Vishnu, and the sixty-three Nayanars, devoted to Shiva. Among them were a woman, Andal, and men of the lowest castes.

From there it moved north, changing as it went:

  • Karnataka, 12th century: Basava and the Lingayats rejected caste and the priesthood.
  • Maharashtra, 13th to 17th century: Jnaneshwar, Namdev and Tukaram sang to Vithoba at Pandharpur.
  • The north, 15th and 16th century: Kabir the weaver, Mirabai, Surdas and Tulsidas, author of the Ramcharitmanas.
  • Bengal: Chaitanya and his dancing, singing followers of Krishna.

The saints made the regional languages into literary ones, and their songs are still sung daily. The movement met Sufism in the north and shaped Guru Nanak, the founder of the Sikh faith. It weakened the hold of caste in worship, though not in daily life.
